person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Verbal multiword expressions - verbal idioms - and the relation between their semantic properties and the syntactic variation they permit.
span.quote: In this chapter we focus on verbal MWEs, often referred to as "verbal idioms" or simply "idioms".

span.label: Is the behaviour of idioms an idiosyncratic property of each idiom, or a consequence of more general constraints?
span.quote: Our primary research question is whether the behavior of idioms is an idiosyncratic property of each idiom or a consequence of more general constraints.

span.label: Replaces decomposability with an alternative categorization that cross-classifies idioms on two dimensions, figuration and transparency.
span.quote: In this chapter we consider an alternative categorization of idioms. More precisely, we cross-classify idioms according to two dimensions: figuration and transparency

span.label: critique
span.quote: we argue that decomposability is not a primitive semantic property of idioms, nor can it be used to predict idioms' behavior.

span.label: idiom flexibility is a continuum rather than a two-way split, with every idiom examined showing some flexibility
span.quote: we hypothesize that idioms cannot be categorically classified as either flexible or rigid. Rather, we envision a continuum with idioms exhibiting varying degrees of flexibility, possibly dependent on their semantic properties.

span.label: corpus study
span.quote: We used heTenTen 2014 (Baroni et al. 2009), a billion-token web-crawled Hebrew corpus, available on SketchEngine (Kilgarriff et al. 2004), to search for different types of variations that occur with representative MWEs from the three semantic classes we outlined in Section 3.1. We focused on fifteen specific verbal MWEs, and annotated 400 examples overall.

span.label: The study reports no quantitative distribution, because the wide-net queries return false positives that only manual inspection can remove.
span.quote: Nevertheless, a wide net comes at a cost; not all the retrieved results are necessarily instances of the idiom. Often, only a manual inspection of each result can weed out the false positives. For this reason we do not present quantitative data with regard to the distribution of the canonical idiom and its variations.

span.label: The generalisation rests on a limited set of Hebrew verbal idioms.
span.quote: Naturally, this generalization, which is based on our work on only a limited set of Hebrew verbal idioms, requires further investigation.

span.label: The criterion under critique is described as impressionistic and circular: flexibility is taken as evidence for the very property meant to predict it.
span.quote: determining whether an idiom is decomposable or not is rather impressionistic, and is prone to circularity, where its flexibility is taken as evidence for its decomposability.

span.label: The originating proposal supplied neither precise definitions of its two categories nor a procedure for telling them apart.
span.quote: Nunberg et al. (1994) do not provide precise definitions for the two categories, or a specific procedure for distinguishing between them.

span.label: An independent corpus study classifying by paraphrase reported the boundary between the two categories as fuzzy.
span.quote: She classified those for which she found an appropriate paraphrase as decomposable. Nevertheless, she observed that the boundary between the two categories is fuzzy.

span.label: Two psycholinguistic studies of the same construct disagree on whether speakers can apply it reliably.
span.quote: In contrast, Titone & Connine (1994) did not find reliable agreement regarding decomposability in their study. Of the 171 idioms which they examined, only 40% were classified into one 38 2 Verbal multiword expressions: Idiomaticity and flexibility of the three categories (normally decomposable, abnormally decomposable nondecomposable) with at least 75% agreement among subjects. The authors suggest that grouping idioms into these categories may rely on a type of linguistic knowledge that is not easily accessed.

span.label: The rigidity of the field's standard example is shown to depend on corpus size; variation appears only in a very large corpus.
span.quote: However, since this idiom is used relatively rarely and idiom variations in and of themselves are relatively infrequent, non-canonical instances of it and other infrequent idioms can only be empirically attested in very large corpora. This, we believe, is an important methodological finding, which at this point in time, with the availability of large annotated corpora, cannot be overlooked.

span.label: The authors' own prediction about cranberry idioms was not borne out, and they say so.
span.quote: We were especially surprised by the behavior of the cranberry idioms. Our initial expectation was that the lack of transparency and figuration would render these idioms more rigid. Our corpus findings, however, reveal a different picture.

span.label: Neither proposed dimension accounts for idiom behaviour on its own; the paper attributes the effect to an interaction.
span.quote: Thus, we propose that neither transparency nor figuration alone can account for the behavior of idioms. Our findings suggest that there is an interaction between the two dimensions.

span.label: decomposability - Nunberg et al.'s sense: an idiom whose meaning, once known, can be distributed among its parts
span.quote: The former are idioms whose meaning, once known, can be distributed among their parts. A typical example is spill the beans, where spill roughly means `reveal' and beans roughly means `secrets'.

span.label: transparency - the relation between an idiom's literal and idiomatic meaning, which the source proposal explicitly warns must not be confused with decomposability
span.quote: They do however explicitly warn against confusing decomposability with transparency, which they define as the relation between the literal and idiomatic meaning.

span.label: paraphrasability - whether the idiom can be paraphrased by a similarly structured phrase, explicitly distinguished from decomposability
span.quote: An additional distinction is made between decomposability and paraphrasability. The fact that the meaning of an idiom can be paraphrased using a phrase of a similar argument structure does not necessarily indicate that it is decomposable.

span.label: flexibility - the categorical sense inherited from Nunberg et al., on which an idiom is either transformationally productive or transformationally deficient
span.quote: They propose that the semantic distinction between decomposable and non-decomposable idioms accounts for the difference between "transformationally productive" and "transformationally deficient" idioms.

span.label: flexibility - this paper's sense: a continuum, with idioms exhibiting varying degrees rather than falling into two classes
span.quote: Rather, we envision a continuum with idioms exhibiting varying degrees of flexibility, possibly dependent on their semantic properties.

span.label: figuration - the degree to which the idiom can be assigned a literal meaning that conjures a picture
span.quote: Figuration reflects the degree to which the idiom can be assigned a literal meaning. Transparency (or opacity) relates to how easy it is to recover the motivation for an idiom's use, or, in other words, to explain the relationship between its literal meaning and its idiomatic one.

span.label: decomposability —distinct-from→ transparency
span.quote: They do however explicitly warn against confusing decomposability with transparency, which they define as the relation between the literal and idiomatic meaning.

span.label: decomposability —distinct-from→ paraphrasability
span.quote: An additional distinction is made between decomposability and paraphrasability. The fact that the meaning of an idiom can be paraphrased using a phrase of a similar argument structure does not necessarily indicate that it is decomposable.

span.label: verbal idioms —part-of→ multiword expressions
span.quote: In this chapter we focus on verbal MWEs, often referred to as "verbal idioms" or simply "idioms".

span.label: figuration —distinct-from→ transparency
span.quote: In this chapter we consider an alternative categorization of idioms. More precisely, we cross-classify idioms according to two dimensions: figuration and transparency

span.label: cranberry idioms —contrasted-with→ figuration
span.quote: Idioms which are not figurative do not have a comprehensible literal meaning, and as such are necessarily opaque. Among these idioms we find what are referred to as "cranberry idioms" (Moon 1998; Trawinski et al. 2008), which, similarly to "cranberry morphemes", have parts which have no meanings

span.label: The paper's central question is whether idiom behaviour is idiosyncratic or predictable from general constraints.
span.quote: Is information regarding their flexibility encoded for each idiom individually, or can the behavior of idioms be predicted from general principles?

span.label: Idioms are not uniformly rigid; some keep their idiomatic meaning outside their canonical form.
span.quote: Not all idioms, however, are equally rigid, as some maintain their idiomatic meaning even when they do not appear in their canonical form.

span.label: semantic idiomaticity
span.quote: their meaning cannot be systematically derived from the meanings that their parts have when they are used independently
